Independent Public Record

Cornell's Own Records

Cornell's public records document the reported assault, the university's response and the institutional history of the Chi Phi Xi chapter before Jane Doe filed the September 2026 civil lawsuit.

Official Cornell Governance Record November 2024
01

Student Assembly Resolution 17

Cornell University Office of the Assemblies

Before the civil lawsuit was filed, Cornell's Student Assembly placed the reported assault into the university's own public record through Resolution 17.

The resolution refers directly to the Crime Alert sent to the Cornell community on November 8, 2024. It says the alert described a Cornell undergraduate who had been sexually assaulted and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs in the 100 block of Edgemoor Lane in Ithaca.

The resolution was adopted by the Student Assembly and its official Cornell page lists its status as acknowledged by the president.

From the Cornell record

“Sexually assaulted and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs.”

Record note: Resolution 17 dates the incident described in Cornell's Crime Alert to October 25, 2024. The September 2026 civil complaint places the alleged assault on the night of October 19 into the morning of October 20. CornellSeven.com has not located a public record explaining the difference between those dates.

Official Cornell Statement November 26, 2024
02

Cornell Publicly Addresses the Chi Phi Investigation

Office of the President · Cornell University

Less than three weeks after the November 8 Crime Alert, then- Interim President Michael Kotlikoff issued a university-wide statement addressing the reports from the Chi Phi house.

Cornell said that a number of students had been temporarily suspended and that Chi Phi remained temporarily suspended while the criminal investigation continued. The university also said its student-conduct and Title IX offices were reviewing the information that had been reported about events at the fraternity.

The statement documents Cornell's response at the time, nearly two years before Jane Doe filed the civil complaint now at the center of this site.

Cornell's words

“Only those who perpetrate sexual violence benefit from its concealment.”

Official Cornell Organization Record · Historical Context 2018–2024
03

Chi Phi Had a Documented Conduct History Before 2024

Cornell Student & Campus Life · Cornell Public Records · Cornell Daily Sun

Cornell's official organization scorecard identifies Chi Phi's Xi chapter at 107 Edgemoor Lane, identifies the fraternity house as university-owned, and currently lists the chapter's recognition status as Interim Suspension.

The 2024 allegations did not arrive at a chapter with a spotless disciplinary record. Cornell's own organization scorecard documents repeated findings against Chi Phi's Xi chapter years before Jane Doe's report, including hazing, alcohol violations, overcrowding, inadequate sober monitoring and broader organizational misconduct.

The students occupying the house changed over time. The chapter did not. Cornell treated these matters as organizational violations, imposed chapter-wide sanctions and, in several instances, required education or corrective measures reaching the membership as a whole. That history is relevant when examining the culture and risk-management record of the organization itself rather than pretending October 2024 appeared out of nowhere.

2018 Chi Phi · Cornell Finding

Hazing, hard liquor and alcohol provided to people under 21

Cornell found Chi Phi responsible for a hazing violation, a recruitment or new-member function violation, hard liquor and selling or giving alcohol to people under 21. Sanctions included probationary recognition, a revised orientation plan and social probation.

March 2020 Chi Phi · Event Management

Overcrowding and insufficient sober monitors

Cornell found Chi Phi responsible for exceeding assembly-space occupancy limits and having insufficient sober monitors. The chapter was also cited for failing to prevent overcrowding and was required to complete training.

April 2020 Chi Phi · Collective Responsibility

Cornell held the chapter responsible for members' conduct

In a separate matter, Cornell cited Chi Phi for collective responsibility for the behavior of its members inside and outside the chapter house, along with property conditions, unreasonable noise and compliance with local laws. Cornell required the chapter to document corrective measures and internal consequences.

Nov. 2022 Cornell Greek System · Campus-Wide Crisis

Drugging and sexual-assault reports shut down IFC social events

Cornell's fraternity system entered a campus-wide crisis after multiple reports of drugging and a sexual-assault allegation at fraternity-affiliated residences. The IFC suspended fraternity parties and social events for the remainder of the fall semester. Cornell Student Assembly records from the same period referenced reports involving suspected Rohypnol exposure and sexual assault.

Public reporting identified other fraternities in connection with the 2022 allegations; this entry is not presented as a Chi Phi-specific accusation. It documents the wider Greek-life environment in which the Classes of 2023 and 2024 were active.

Feb. 2023 Cornell IFC · Safety Overhaul

Consent training, risk controls and upgraded sober-monitor duties

When fraternity social events resumed, Cornell and the IFC imposed new requirements involving sexual-violence prevention, consent and bystander-intervention training, event checks and upgraded sober-monitor responsibilities. Chapter leaders and advisors were required to sign off on policy knowledge and risk-management plans before events resumed.

April 2023 Chi Phi · Cornell Finding

Another Chi Phi organizational-misconduct finding

Cornell again found Chi Phi responsible for misconduct related to the organization, citing prohibited conduct involving public urination and garbage. The response went far beyond a warning: Cornell required a decision-making course, a facilitated Culture of Respect dialogue for the chapter and facility, a Gorge Stewardship course built into new-member education and required for all current members, a sustainability workshop, leadership-transition documentation and a chapter sustainability plan.

2024 Chi Phi · Sexual Assault & Drugging Report

Cornell suspends Chi Phi after a sexual-assault and drugging report

Cornell University Police received a report involving sexual assault, several males, ketamine and other drugs at a fraternity in the 100 block of Edgemoor Lane. Cornell subsequently confirmed that Chi Phi was the suspended fraternity. The allegations later became the subject of the 2026 civil complaint documented throughout this page.

The Historical Record

Whatever changed from class to class, Chi Phi's institutional record did not begin in October 2024. Cornell had already documented years of chapter-level misconduct and event-management failures.

Why the historical roster matters: CornellSeven.com preserves archived Chi Phi membership across these years because the organization itself has a documented history spanning multiple graduating classes. The 2023 sanctions are especially relevant to the Classes of 2023 and 2024 because Cornell directed corrective measures at the chapter and, in one instance, explicitly required participation by all current members. Listing a person in the historical roster does not mean that person personally committed any of the underlying violations.
Leadership continuity: Undergraduate officers change as students graduate, but Chi Phi's own governance page describes its Chapter House Association as the primary alumni interface between the active chapter and Cornell, responsible for advising the chapter and handling operational issues and budgets. The current page lists Rob Shuck as president of that association. That is an institutional oversight structure designed to continue across graduating classes.
Source distinction: The 2018, 2020 and 2023 entries above are Chi Phi-specific Cornell disciplinary records. The November 2022 drugging and sexual-assault reports involved the broader Cornell fraternity system and public reporting identified other fraternities in connection with those reports. They are included here as campus and Greek-life context, not as an accusation that Chi Phi caused those 2022 incidents.

Current Case Developments

Recent Developments

The criminal investigation has moved beyond the Tompkins County District Attorney. On October 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the New York Attorney General's Office as special prosecutor. By October 2, additional reporting had surfaced a 565-page set of Cornell Title IX interview records, an extended version of the Chi Phi Actives Snapchat chain, a photograph of Jane Doe shared into that group during the night, additional witness accounts and newly unsealed disciplinary-court records. Cornell has separately agreed to an outside review of its institutional response, while the Attorney General's criminal investigation is beginning under a separate mandate.

Criminal Investigation · Special Prosecutor · State Action September 27–October 2, 2026
04

Criminal Case Reopened, Then Transferred to the New York Attorney General

Tompkins County District Attorney · Gov. Kathy Hochul · New York Attorney General · Associated Press

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten first announced that his office was reopening its review of the alleged October 2024 assault after the September 2026 civil lawsuit brought additional evidence and renewed scrutiny to the case. He said prosecutors intended to prepare the matter for presentation to a grand jury.

On October 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced a major change in who will control that criminal review. Hochul said newly released information raised serious questions about both the Cornell University Police investigation and the earlier decision not to prosecute. She signed an executive order appointing the Office of New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor for this case.

The Attorney General's office confirmed the appointment the same evening. Under the order, James's office will now oversee the criminal investigation and, if the evidence warrants it, may present the case to a grand jury.

Current Criminal-Case Status

The reopened criminal investigation is now being led by the New York Attorney General's Office as special prosecutor.

What changed: Van Houten remains the elected Tompkins County District Attorney, but the criminal investigation documented on this page is no longer under his control. At an October 2 news conference, Attorney General Letitia James said her office would review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted. She said a comprehensive investigation would take time and suggested the work could extend for months. No criminal charge or indictment had been announced as of the October 2 update through 3 p.m. Pacific.

2024 Police Interview Transcript · CBS News · Associated Press · WSKG November 14–15, 2024 · Reported Sept. 30–Oct. 1, 2026
05

Full Police Interview Shows Jane Doe Explicitly Described Rape, Coercion and Incapacitation

Cornell University Police Interview Transcript · CBS News New York · Associated Press · WSKG

CBS News obtained the transcript of Jane Doe's detailed interviews with Cornell University Police on November 14 and 15, 2024. Subsequent reporting described that interview record as roughly 120 pages, compared with a much shorter written statement that was provided to prosecutors.

The transcript shows Jane Doe distinguishing sexual activity she initially described as consensual from conduct she said happened later. She described repeated pressure as coercion, said she had been hit and said she became “completely and totally incapacitated.”

Jane Doe's 2024 Police Interview

“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”

Van Houten said he had not seen the complete interview transcript when his office declined to prosecute the case in 2024. He said prosecutors instead relied on a shorter statement prepared through Cornell Police, which did not contain Jane Doe's unequivocal statement that she had been raped.

After the transcript became public, Van Houten told WSKG that, if the reported transcript was accurate, it would have changed the investigation and that his office should have been told about material from Jane Doe's police interview that was missing from the shorter statement.

Why this matters: The transcript directly complicates the earlier public explanation that Jane Doe's 2024 account did not allege forced sex or incapacitation. Her full police interview contained explicit statements about rape, coercion and incapacity that the prosecutor says he did not receive before the original decision not to bring charges.

Post-Incident Communications · Medical Visits · Internal Cornell Records October–November 2024 · Reported October 1, 2026
06

Contemporary Records Trace Jane Doe's Shift From Shock and Shame to Reporting an Assault

Cornell Internal Investigation Records · New York Times · Associated Press · People

Newly reported Cornell investigation records provide a much fuller chronology of the weeks between the night at Chi Phi and Jane Doe's report to campus police. They show that her understanding of what had happened changed over a short period while she was also dealing with physical symptoms, campus rumors and increasing distress.

According to the records, one of the men later named in the lawsuit apologized soon after the incident for how the night had unfolded and said that he and another fraternity member regretted being too intoxicated to stop the situation before it got out of hand. Jane Doe initially said she did not think the sexual activity had been illegal.

The records also document actions Jane Doe took before the 2026 lawsuit. Reporting says she preserved the dress she had been wearing rather than washing it, photographed bruising she attributed to the night, went to Cornell Health two days later for UTI and STI-related care and described the infection as having occurred in a “traumatic way.”

November 3, 2024

Jane Doe told Johnathan Newell that “90% of what happened that night was not consensual.”

She also wrote that she had been given more ketamine than she could remember and reminded Newell that she had said she felt uncomfortable and did not know the people in the room. On November 7, the newly reported records say she went to an Ithaca emergency room and requested a rape-kit examination. She reported the incident to Cornell University Police the following day.

During the detailed police interview that followed, Jane Doe explicitly said she had been raped. The chronology places her medical care, evidence preservation, nonconsensual description and rape-kit request in 2024, nearly two years before she filed the civil lawsuit.

Context for the earliest messages: Defense statements have emphasized Jane Doe's first texts after the incident. The broader contemporaneous record shows that those messages were followed within days by escalating distress, medical care, preserved evidence, a written statement that most of the night was nonconsensual, a requested rape kit and a police report.

Evidence Transfer Dispute · Cornell FAQ · District Attorney · WSKG September 29–October 2, 2026
07

Cornell Changes Its Public Account of What Police Shared With Prosecutors

Cornell University · Tompkins County District Attorney · Cornell Daily Sun · WSKG

Cornell initially published an FAQ stating that Cornell University Police had shared “all investigatory information” with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office in 2024. That statement conflicted with Van Houten's public assertion that his office had never received the fraternity Snapchat evidence reproduced in the civil complaint.

The conflict widened when Van Houten said he also had never seen Jane Doe's complete police-interview transcript and had instead relied on a much shorter written statement.

Cornell then removed the “all investigatory information” language from its FAQ. After WSKG reported on that deletion, Cornell changed the page again on October 1. The new language specifically says CUPD shared Jane Doe's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the district attorney.

The Conflict Now

Cornell specifically says the Snapchat screenshot was sent. Van Houten said his office did not receive it, and he said he never saw the full police-interview transcript.

The latest Cornell wording is narrower than its original claim. It identifies two specific items — the sworn statement and Snapchat screenshot — but does not say the district attorney received Jane Doe's complete police-interview transcript.

On October 2, The Cornell Daily Sun published its own comparison of the FAQ versions and documented at least two edits to Cornell's answer. The same day, after the case had been transferred to the Attorney General, Van Houten said he supported the appointment and stated that his office had not been provided the full picture by the University.

What remains unresolved: The public record still does not establish where the evidence-transfer breakdown occurred or why the prosecutor reviewing the case says he did not receive material Cornell says was sent. On October 1, the criminal investigation was transferred from Van Houten to the New York Attorney General's Office as special prosecutor.

The Cornell Daily Sun

“Almost two years later, I still carry the weight of its impact every day and night.”

Official Cornell Statement September 21, 2026
09

Cornell Confirms Its Investigation Has Concluded

Cornell University · Office of University Relations

On September 21, 2026, Cornell publicly confirmed that its investigation into the alleged 2024 incident at the Chi Phi house had concluded.

Vice President for University Relations Kyle Kimball said Cornell's Office of Civil Rights and Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated and adjudicated the allegations under university policies.

Cornell also confirmed that the Xi chapter of Chi Phi continues to be barred from campus.

Cornell's Current Position

Chi Phi “remains barred from our campus.”

Cornell declined to disclose disciplinary consequences involving individual students. The university cited federal student-privacy law and said it is prohibited from publicly releasing specific information about individual disciplinary responses.

Cornell stated that violations of university policy can result in sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion, but did not publicly identify what sanctions were imposed on any individual student connected to the investigation.

Record update: The Sept. 21 statement independently confirmed that Cornell's university investigation was no longer pending. On Sept. 28, Cornell went further and confirmed that the completed process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, while still declining to identify individual outcomes.

Cornell Disciplinary Outcomes · CBS News · Defense Disclosure September 28–October 1, 2026
10

Cornell's Seven Outcomes: Two Expelled, Two Suspended, Two Found Not Responsible, One Graduated

Cornell University · President Michael Kotlikoff · CBS News · Gillio Lopes's Attorney

Cornell first said its completed Title IX and student-conduct process resulted in a range of sanctions that included expulsions and suspensions, while declining to identify individual outcomes.

CBS News later reported that President Michael Kotlikoff gave student government a more precise breakdown on September 29: two of the seven were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before Cornell could impose a sanction, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct.

Cornell still has not publicly matched those outcomes to individual names. One individual outcome has now been disclosed by a defendant's own attorney: Tara Davis said Gillio Lopes was suspended by Cornell and received additional educational sanctions.

Davis also said Lopes had sexual contact with Jane Doe but maintains that it was consensual. That defense account is addressed separately in the defendant-statements record below.

The Seven Reported Outcomes

2 expelled · 2 suspended for at least two semesters · 1 graduated before sanction · 2 found not responsible for sexual misconduct.

What remains undisclosed: Cornell itself has not publicly identified which respondent received each result. The Lopes suspension is attributed to his own attorney, not to a university disclosure naming him.

Investigation & Accountability

What Happened After Jane Doe Reported?

Public statements from Cornell, prosecutors and local police now provide a clearer — and in some places disputed — picture of what happened after Jane Doe reported the alleged assault.

Cross-Referenced Public Record 2024–October 1, 2026
12

The Investigation Chain

Civil Complaint · CUPD · District Attorney · Cornell · IPD · CBS News · WSKG · New York Attorney General

Jane Doe's civil complaint says she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on or about November 8, 2024. Cornell issued a Crime Alert that day and temporarily suspended the fraternity connected to the report.

Cornell Police conducted a lengthy interview with Jane Doe on November 14 and 15. Reporting on the transcript shows that she told the investigator she had been raped, described coercion and said she had become completely incapacitated.

Van Houten later said his office relied on Cornell Police's work when declining charges in 2024, did not conduct a separate investigation and did not receive Jane Doe's complete interview transcript. He also said his office did not receive the fraternity Snapchat evidence.

Cornell's public account has changed during the renewed scrutiny. Its FAQ initially said CUPD provided prosecutors with all investigatory information, then removed that language, and on October 1 specifically stated that CUPD shared Jane Doe's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the district attorney.

Ithaca Police has said the incident was never reported to its department. Van Houten reopened the criminal case in late September 2026, but on October 1 Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the Office of Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor. James's office now controls the renewed criminal investigation.

The Documented Sequence

CUPD report → detailed interview → 2024 prosecutor review → no charges → civil lawsuit → evidence-transfer conflict → case reopened → Attorney General appointed special prosecutor.

Central unresolved issue: The public record still leaves unanswered exactly what evidence Cornell Police collected, what was transmitted to prosecutors in 2024 and why the full police-interview account was not before the prosecutor who made the original charging decision.

Cornell's Policy 6.4 Procedures in Effect at the Time

Cornell Office of Civil Rights

Cornell's Office of Civil Rights preserves the student procedures under Policy 6.4 that became effective Aug. 5, 2024 — before the alleged October 2024 incident and before Jane Doe's report.

Cornell identifies those procedures as the process applicable to student respondents accused of sexual misconduct during the period before the university adopted newer procedures in 2026.

That policy record gives readers a contemporaneous framework for evaluating Cornell's written procedures separately from the allegations in Jane Doe's lawsuit about how the university actually handled her case.

Important distinction: The existence of a written procedure does not establish whether Cornell followed that procedure in Jane Doe's case. The civil lawsuit's institutional claims remain allegations being litigated.

Institutional Context

Campus and Greek-Life Context

Cornell's own data and public records provide broader context about sexual assault on campus, the disproportionate prevalence reported by women affiliated with Greek life, and the university fraternity system's response after the 2024 Chi Phi report.

Official Cornell Task Force Report March 2026
15

Cornell's Task Force Identifies Elevated Risk in Greek Life

Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault

In March 2026, Cornell's Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault issued its final report examining sexual assault among undergraduate students and recommending changes to prevention, education, campus culture and institutional response.

Among the report's most striking findings was a major difference between women who were affiliated with Greek life and women who were not.

52% of Greek-affiliated undergraduate women respondents reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell.
29% of undergraduate women respondents who were not affiliated with Greek life reported experiencing sexual assault.

The task force also reported that fraternity chapter houses accounted for 17% of the locations identified for reported sexual assaults in the 2025 survey. Residence halls were the most commonly identified location at 29%, followed by off-campus residences at 23%.

Cornell Task Force Finding

The prevalence reported among Greek-affiliated undergraduate women was nearly twice that reported among women who were not Greek-affiliated.

In response, the task force recommended required annual in-person training on consent and sexual citizenship for prospective new members and active fraternity and sorority members.

It also recommended annual in-person, situation-based training for fraternity and sorority leaders because of the role those students play in shaping chapter culture and responding to potentially dangerous situations.

Survey limitation: Cornell's task force emphasized that the undergraduate response rate to the 2025 survey was only 13%, down from 34% in 2023. The report states that the low response rate limits estimates of sexual assault and makes the results more difficult to interpret.

Official Cornell Survey November 4, 2025
16

Cornell Reports Rising Sexual-Misconduct Numbers

Cornell Survey of Sexual Assault and Related Misconduct

Cornell released the results of its 2025 Survey of Sexual Assault and Related Misconduct on November 4, 2025.

The university reported an increase in the percentage of respondents who said they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving at Cornell.

35% of undergraduate women respondents reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact during their Cornell careers, compared with 23% in 2023.
15% of all 2025 respondents reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since coming to Cornell, compared with 11% in 2023.

Cornell also reported that nearly half of respondents — 49% — said they had experienced sexual or gender-based harassment. That figure had been 45% in the university's 2023 survey.

Reporting and Support

Only 23% of 2025 respondents who reported nonconsensual sexual contact said they contacted a formal resource.

Cornell said many students who did not seek formal help indicated that they believed what happened was not serious enough to report or address through official channels.

The university said the results would be used to guide prevention programs, support services and its broader effort to address sexual violence on campus.

Participation rate: Cornell sent the 2025 survey to a random sample of 6,000 undergraduate, graduate and professional students across its campuses. A total of 926 students participated, producing an overall response rate of 15%. Cornell cautioned that the low response rate and unanswered demographic questions make the 2025 estimates less certain than previous survey results.

Contemporary Campus Reporting November 15, 2024
17

Cornell Greek Life Responds After the Chi Phi Report

Cornell Interfraternity Council · The Cornell Daily Sun

One week after the reported sexual assault and drugging that led Cornell to suspend Chi Phi, the university's Interfraternity Council voted unanimously to suspend fraternity social activity for the weekend.

The Cornell Daily Sun reported that approximately 100 fraternity leaders representing all 29 IFC chapters met for several hours to discuss the Chi Phi suspension and the fraternity system's response.

IFC Public Response

The council said all forms of sexual misconduct were unacceptable and expressed sympathy to the survivor or survivors.

In addition to the temporary suspension of social events, the IFC unanimously approved mandatory sexual-assault-prevention training for every fraternity beginning the following semester.

The response came in November 2024, while the criminal and university investigations connected to the Chi Phi report were still underway and nearly two years before Jane Doe filed her civil lawsuit.

Why this record matters: The IFC action documents the scale of the immediate reaction inside Cornell's fraternity system. The response involved every IFC chapter and occurred within days of the original public report, long before the allegations became the subject of the September 2026 civil lawsuit.

Contemporary Public Record

The First Public Report

The November 2024 Crime Alert provides a contemporaneous record of what Cornell told its community immediately after the alleged assault was reported to university police.

Cornell Crime Alert · Contemporary Reporting November 8, 2024
18

Cornell Issues Crime Alert After Report of Sexual Assault and Drugging

Cornell University Police · The Cornell Daily Sun

On November 8, 2024, Cornell distributed a Crime Alert to the university community after an undergraduate student reported being sexually assaulted and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs.

The alert said the reported incident involved several males and occurred at a fraternity in the 100 block of Edgemoor Lane in Ithaca.

Cornell University Police had been notified by the individual that day. According to the alert, the fraternity connected to the report was placed on temporary suspension effective immediately while the investigation continued.

Cornell's Public Record

Cornell described a report involving a student who was “sexually assaulted and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs.”

The initial Crime Alert did not publicly identify which fraternity had been suspended. At the time, The Cornell Daily Sun noted that the two fraternity houses on the 100 block of Edgemoor Lane were Chi Phi and Lambda Chi Alpha.

Lambda Chi Alpha's president told The Sun that the chapter had no knowledge of the situation. Cornell declined to identify the fraternity under investigation when asked by the newspaper.

Subsequent Cornell communications confirmed that Chi Phi was the fraternity that had been suspended. By November 26, Cornell publicly stated that Chi Phi remained temporarily suspended while the criminal investigation continued.

Date discrepancy: The November 8 Crime Alert described the reported incident as occurring on October 25, 2024. Cornell's Student Assembly later repeated that date in Resolution 17. Jane Doe's September 2026 civil complaint instead places the alleged events overnight on October 19–20, 2024. The public records reviewed here do not explain the difference between those dates.
Why this record matters: This alert predates the civil lawsuit by nearly two years. It documents that a report involving sexual assault, multiple males, ketamine and other drugs was made to Cornell University Police in November 2024 and that Cornell immediately suspended a fraternity in response.

Jane Doe's lawsuit and public comments have also prompted responses from the Cornell community, the campus newspaper's editorial board and public officials. These entries are clearly identified as commentary or attributed public statements rather than findings of fact.

Campus Editorial · Opinion September 21, 2026

Cornell Daily Sun Editorial Demands Greater Accountability

The Cornell Daily Sun Editorial Board

In an editorial titled Cornell Won't, We Will, the Cornell Daily Sun editorial board centered Jane Doe's loss of safety and education and argued that student safety is fundamental to the university's educational mission.

The editorial raised questions about transparency surrounding Cornell's Title IX process, the duration of temporary suspensions and what information the university has made available about the handling of the case.

The editorial is opinion, not an official Cornell finding. It is included here because it documents a significant campus response to Jane Doe's allegations and the university's handling of them.

Public Official Remarks · Attributed Statement September 27, 2026
20

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Addresses Jane Doe's Case in Ithaca

Ithaca Town Hall · The Cornell Daily Sun

During a Sept. 27 town hall in Ithaca, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez discussed Jane Doe's lawsuit and described the case as part of what she characterized as a broader culture enabling sexual violence at elite institutions.

Ocasio-Cortez focused on the educational consequences Jane Doe says she experienced after the alleged assault and criticized institutions that, in her view, protect spaces in which sexual violence can be normalized.

28

Internal Cornell Files Reveal the Men's Own Accounts of the Night

New York Times · Cornell Title IX Investigation Records · CBS News · Public Defense Statements

The New York Times obtained hundreds of pages from Cornell's internal investigation, including interviews with six of the seven men later named in Jane Doe's lawsuit. The Times reported that four of the men acknowledged sexual contact with Jane Doe while maintaining that the interactions were consensual; the others denied sexual encounters. The Times described their accounts as sometimes contradictory to one another and generally at odds with Jane Doe's account to police.

Johnathan Newell told Cornell investigators that Matthew Ingalls invited him into a threesome. Newell said he and Ingalls had consumed alcohol, marijuana and ketamine heavily enough that both vomited.

Winston Lee told investigators that he snorted a line of ketamine from Jane Doe's body. He said she attempted to initiate sexual activity, claimed he initially stepped back and later acknowledged participating in a threesome that he maintained was consensual.

Gillio Lopes acknowledged sexual contact with Jane Doe but said she initiated it. He told investigators he later became uncomfortable and left for McDonald's, and said he was embarrassed about what had happened. On October 1, his attorney Tara Davis publicly repeated that Lopes had sexual contact with Jane Doe while maintaining that it was consensual.

Scott Kretzschmar told investigators that Newell's Snapchat message left him “befuddled” before he and Scott Norris entered the room. Norris said the message made him “somewhat concerned” but that he interpreted it as crude humor. Both denied sexual activity with Jane Doe.

Diego Sarabia told investigators he was “immensely concerned” when he entered the room because he had never seen anything like it in four years living at the house. He said his concern later eased after people in the room told him to enter.

Defense positions remain denials of wrongdoing: These statements are the men's accounts, not findings that their versions are true. The new reporting is significant because it documents, in their own interviews, admissions of sexual contact, ketamine use, presence in the room and contemporaneous concern that go well beyond a simple claim that they had no connection to what was happening.
Gillio Lopes's October 1 public defense: Davis also said Lopes did not use ketamine and was not part of the controversial Snapchat group, and disclosed that Cornell suspended him and imposed additional educational sanctions. Those are claims and disclosures made by his attorney; Cornell has not publicly identified Lopes's individual disciplinary outcome by name.

37

Extended Snapchat Chain Shows a Photo of Jane Doe and Additional Messages

CBS News · ABC News · The Washington Post · Cornell Title IX Records

The screenshot reproduced in the civil complaint is not the full Snapchat exchange. On October 2, multiple national outlets reported that they had obtained or reviewed additional portions of the Chi Phi Actives conversation from the night of the alleged assault.

CBS News reported that a photograph of Jane Doe with another man was shared into the group during the night. Immediately before the photo, a participant wrote, “Like you can walk in and whip it out.” Immediately after the photo, another participant asked “Shop still open?” and received the response “Yeah.”

ABC News reported that it obtained an extended version of the group chat. ABC said the fraternity brother who invited Jane Doe to the house sent a photograph that appeared to show her in the bedroom. Another participant asked, “Are you guys at least naked??” and the inviting brother later wrote, “Boys come whip it out.” The Washington Post separately reported that a screen recording it obtained also contained the photograph and additional messages.

Cornell's Title IX records add important context about the size of the audience. CBS reported that a participant identified as “Male 6” told investigators that about 50 fraternity members were on that particular Snapchat thread. ABC described the extended chat as being shared among more than 50 fraternity brothers.

What the New Material Establishes

The public record now includes more than the single complaint screenshot: major news organizations have reviewed additional messages, a photograph shared in the group and a longer recording of the exchange.

Group-size distinction: Reporting reviewed through 3 p.m. Pacific on October 2 does not establish that the Snapchat thread contained exactly 57 people. CBS reports that a fraternity member described about 50 people on the particular thread, while ABC describes more than 50. A separate count of active fraternity members should not automatically be treated as the exact Snapchat-thread membership without additional evidence.
Unresolved first-name account: The complaint screenshot includes a visible participant identified only as “Ryan.” Public reporting reviewed for this update does not establish that person's surname. CornellSeven.com is not assigning that account to a particular Ryan without corroborating evidence.

38

565 Pages of Title IX Records Add Witness, Ketamine and First-Report Details

Cornell Title IX Investigation Records · CBS News · CBS New York · ABC News

CBS News reported that it obtained 565 pages of transcripts from Cornell's Title IX investigation. Cornell's 2025 process included about 50 interviews with 32 witnesses. A CBS New York report on the same record said the material included Jane Doe's account, interviews with six of the seven men named in the lawsuit and 20 witnesses.

One new detail concerns ketamine at the beginning of the night. A man identified by CBS as “Male 2” told Cornell investigators that he and “Male 1” took ketamine during the initial sexual encounter but that Jane Doe declined the drug at that point.

Another witness told investigators that one of the accused men called her the day after the alleged assault and asked her to make sure a friend did not say anything about what she thought might have happened the night before. The witness said the caller added that another fraternity member was very concerned. CBS did not publicly identify the accused man who allegedly made that call.

According to the transcript, that man initially denied having the call. In later written corrections, he acknowledged speaking to the student about not spreading rumors. In the same interview, he described the fraternity brothers' approach to the rumors as “just deny.”

A friend of the witness and her roommate said they later went to Cornell Police. One said she wrote a witness statement. CBS reported that the disposition of that statement is not referenced in the 565 pages the network obtained.

ABC News also reported that the first police report memorialized Jane Doe's allegation as a report that she had been raped by 8–10 men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. ABC reviewed video from Cornell's investigation showing the bedroom weeks later, including discarded items, alcohol containers and a fentanyl test on the floor.

Why this matters: The newly reported file is much larger than the six-page sworn statement that prosecutors say they relied on in 2024. It also contains witness material, statements from accused students and evidence about the sequence of events that was not visible in the original public record.

Unsealed Records Show Scott Kretzschmar Challenged Cornell's Disciplinary Finding

New York Court Records · The Washington Post · Reporting on Unsealed Cornell Proceedings

Newly unsealed court records provide a separate window into Cornell's disciplinary process involving Scott Kretzschmar. Reporting on the records says he challenged Cornell's decision after a 12-day evidentiary hearing and an unsuccessful University appeal.

The disciplinary panel did not find Kretzschmar responsible for the charged offenses of sexual assault or sexual exploitation. It instead found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation, based on findings connected to his seeing the fraternity Snapchat message and then entering the room.

Kretzschmar has argued in court that Cornell did not give him sufficient notice that attempted sexual exploitation was an offense he could be found responsible for in the proceeding. A lower court dismissed his challenge, and reporting says he filed a notice of appeal.

Important distinction: This disciplinary record cuts in more than one direction and is preserved here in full context: Cornell did not find Kretzschmar responsible for sexual assault or sexual exploitation in that proceeding, but did find him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation. His court challenge contests the fairness and notice associated with that finding.

Op-Ed: Building Better Predatory Men

OP-ED · HISTORICAL CONTEXT

BUILDING BETTER PREDATORY MEN

“Truth Dishonesty, Honor Contempt, and Personal Integrity Corruption.”

Share This Op-Ed Email Facebook X Reddit

The allegations surrounding Chi Phi should not be examined as if this fraternity never had issues. Public reporting dating back more than two decades raises serious concerns about the culture that Chi Phi’s own alumni leadership has tolerated and uplifted.

In 2005, GQ profiled Rob Shuck, then a 31-year-old Cornell undergraduate who had enrolled in 1993 and had spent over a decade living in the basement of the Chi Phi fraternity house. The profile portrayed Shuck’s extended undergraduate life as something of a campus legend. His annual birthday celebration had grown into a 150-person wine tour centered heavily around drinking. Shuck also openly discussed having dated an 18-year-old Cornell freshman the previous year, when he was 30. He acknowledged that their age difference eventually became an issue. It begs the question, how many other teenagers did this adult attempt to groom?

Two years later, the Cornell Daily Sun reported that Shuck was still taking classes and still living in Chi Phi’s basement at age 32, roughly thirteen years after first enrolling at Cornell. By then, his prolonged fraternity lifestyle had become so well known that he had been featured in GQ, appeared on The View, and become the subject of a short documentary titled 32 Yr. Old Frat Boy. Once again, this grown adult man’s behavior was being glorified. It was as if they didn’t want us to realize how incredibly creepy it was for him to be living in a house with teens and young, immature, vulnerable adults.

This history matters because Shuck did not simply fade away as an eccentric former fraternity member. In 2006, while he was still a longtime undergraduate, the Cornell Daily Sun identified him as Chi Phi’s chapter advisor. Years later, Cornell records identified him as president of the Chi Phi Chapter House Association. Today, Chi Phi’s own website lists him in that same leadership position. The Chapter House Association says it advises the active chapter, handles operational matters, represents undergraduate interests, and acts as the primary alumni interface between Chi Phi and Cornell.

That progression is what deserves persecution. A man who spent more than a decade embedded in an undergraduate fraternity environment and publicly discussed dating a freshman half a generation younger than himself should never be glorified. Shuck became nationally known for refusing to grow up and act his age. Chi Phi leadership should have forced him out. They never should have condoned this behavior. He never should have been placed in a position of authority over the chapter.

None of that proves that Shuck knew about or participated in the conduct alleged in the current lawsuit. It does, however, raise a legitimate broader question: What behaviors has Chi Phi historically considered as acceptable? What kinds of boundaries has its leadership chosen to normalize?

What else has this fraternity done that Chi Phi was able to sweep under the rug? My opinion is that this case is only the tip of the iceberg and we are soon going to unravel much more than we ever expected.

Chi Phi’s own national risk-management policy now states that the fraternity will not tolerate or condone sexually abusive behavior and requires members to respect the dignity of others. When an organization has to publicly adopt those standards, its past and present leadership are fair subjects for persecution. That is not only for what they prohibit on paper, but for the culture they have cultivated in practice.
